C004.subject: globalization
C004.object: adoption of digital technologies in developing countries
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: globalization adoption of digital technologies in developing countries]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank Enterprise Surveys and ICT access data for firms in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia (2000-2020) — Provides firm-level panel data on technology adoption correlated with trade and FDI flows, allowing direct testing of whether globalization (measured via trade openness and foreign investment) accelerates digital technology uptake in developing countries.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of digital infrastructure rollout in Kenya (M-Pesa) vs. Bangladesh (mobile banking) with analysis of global supply chains and foreign investment — Enables controlled comparison of globalization's role in technology diffusion, isolating factors like multinational presence and trade integration from domestic policy effects.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on technology transfer via global value chains (e.g., from World Development, Journal of International Business Studies) — Synthesizes existing evidence on mechanisms (e.g., spillovers, standards adoption) and conditions under which globalization accelerates or fails to accelerate digital adoption, helping resolve disputed status.

qualifier.geographic: developing countries in Asia and Africa

C005.subject: globalization
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: globalization technology transfer to developing countries]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank technology diffusion datasets (e.g., WDI patent and royalty data for developing vs. developed countries, 1990-2020) — Provides quantitative evidence on whether globalization correlates with reduced or increased technology transfer flows to developing nations, allowing direct testing of the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of IPR regimes and technology licensing in emerging economies (e.g., India, Brazil, Kenya) post-TRIPS — Examines how globalization-driven intellectual property rules may obstruct technology transfer by raising costs and legal barriers, offering context-specific causal evidence.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical literature on 'technology gap' and dependency theory (e.g., works by Amsden, Wade, or Chang on globalization and late industrialization) — Provides conceptual frameworks that predict globalization can entrench technological asymmetries, helping to interpret empirical findings and refine the hypothesis.

C006.subject: globalization
C006.object: increased innovation in domestic industries in developing countries
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: globalization increased innovation in domestic industries in developing countries]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data on patent filings and R&D expenditure by domestic firms in East Asian and Latin American manufacturing sectors (1990-2020), e.g., from World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) and national statistical agencies. — Quantitative analysis of innovation metrics over time can directly test whether periods of increased globalization (e.g., trade liberalization, FDI inflows) correlate with higher domestic innovation, controlling for other factors.

[PATH:literature] Case study literature on technology spillovers from multinational corporations to local suppliers in countries like China, Brazil, and South Korea, e.g., studies in Journal of International Business Studies or World Development. — Existing qualitative and mixed-method research can provide nuanced evidence on mechanisms (e.g., knowledge transfer, competition effects) and contextual conditions that support or undermine the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of endogenous growth and trade, such as those by Grossman and Helpman (1991) or recent extensions incorporating firm-level heterogeneity. — Formal modeling can clarify under which assumptions globalization fosters domestic innovation (e.g., absorptive capacity, intellectual property protection) and generate testable predictions for empirical work.

qualifier.geographic: developing countries in East Asia and Latin America

C007.subject: globalization
C007.object: domestic industries in developing countries to access export markets and achieve economies of scale
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: globalization domestic industries in developing countries to access export markets and achieve economies of scale]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank Enterprise Surveys (WBES) for East Asian and Southeast Asian developing countries, post-1990s — Provides firm-level data on export participation, market access, and scale of operations, allowing direct testing of whether globalization (e.g., trade liberalization) correlates with increased export market access and economies of scale for domestic industries.

[PATH:literature] Case studies of industrial policy in South Korea and Vietnam (e.g., from journals like World Development or Journal of International Economics) — Comparative case analyses can reveal causal mechanisms and contextual factors (e.g., state support, infrastructure) that mediate whether globalization enables or hinders domestic industries' access to export markets and scale economies, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of trade and industrial organization (e.g., Melitz (2003) model of firm heterogeneity and trade) — Provides a formal framework to predict conditions under which globalization enables firms to achieve economies of scale via export markets, and can be tested against empirical patterns in the specified region and time period.

qualifier.geographic: developing countries in East Asia and Southeast Asia
